title: Privacy & Digital Footprint Map
goal: Your kid finds out what information about them is online, and keeps it safe. They list their accounts, map the trail they leave, sort what's private from what's okay to share, check their settings and usernames with you, and make a family privacy plan for the next time a site or game asks for something.
need: A list of the accounts your family uses
Your logins, so you can check settings together

academics.subject: Life skills
academics.text: deciding what to share, and when to say no

levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

howTo.intro: Stranger-danger scares don't build the skill. Map their real accounts with them, sort what's private together, and practise exactly what to do when something asks for their information.

plan.what: List the accounts and map the footprint (Steps 1 and 2).
Sort, check settings and usernames (Steps 3 and 4).

troubleshoot.a: Ask what a stranger could figure out from their username and one photo. Working it out together usually makes the point.

troubleshoot.q: A game or site keeps asking for information
troubleshoot.a: That's exactly what the plan is for. Practise the answer: stop, don't type it, ask a parent.

troubleshoot.q: They want an account you're not sure about
troubleshoot.a: Map it first: what it asks for, who can see what, who they could talk to. Check its minimum age too; most social apps are 13+. Decide together.

lesson.text: Everything you do online leaves a trail: accounts, usernames, photos, what you search and buy. Some of it you choose to share, and some you don't notice. Knowing what's in your trail, and what stays private, is how you stay safe and in charge.
lesson.before: 'It's only my birthday. What's the harm?'

model.line: A team jersey with the town's name on it.
Her age, her town, her team and her birthday week.

lesson.modelNote: Each piece alone looked harmless. On one page, the username, the jersey and the party post told a stranger her age, town and birthday, and that's the moment the trail stops being okay.

steps.title: List your accounts
steps.why: You can't protect a trail you can't see. The list is the start.
steps.kid: Your kid lists every account they use, with you, using the My accounts card in the Privacy Toolkit at the end of the guide: email, games, reading apps, learning sites.
steps.you: Help them remember the ones you set up for them. Note who made each account and with what information.
ask: Which apps or sites do you log into?
What did each one ask for when it was made?
steps.tip: Include the quiet ones, like an e-reader account, a game login or a voice assistant.

levels.explore: Name the apps you use, and draw a picture for each.
levels.develop: List every account, and what information each one has.
levels.extend: List them, and find out which ones are linked to each other.

steps.title: Map your footprint
steps.why: A map shows how much is out there, and how it connects.
steps.kid: Your kid draws themselves in the middle of a page and adds every account, photo, username and app around them, using the Footprint map card, with lines for what connects.
steps.you: Add the trail grown-ups leave about them too, like photos you've shared. Be honest about yours.
ask: Which part of your map surprised you?
Which accounts know your real name?
steps.tip: Use one colour for things they shared, another for things shared about them by others.

levels.explore: Draw yourself and the apps you use around you.
levels.develop: Map every account, with lines for what's linked.
levels.extend: Map it, then circle what a stranger could find by searching.

steps.title: Sort private from okay
steps.why: Some information is fine to share. Some never is. Knowing the difference is the core skill.
steps.kid: Your kid sorts examples into private, okay with a parent, and fine to share, using the Private or okay? card.
steps.you: Share your own family rules here, and the reasons behind them.
ask: Why is your full name private, but your favourite colour isn't?
What could someone do with your birthday and city?
steps.tip: Combinations matter. A first name alone is fine; a first name, a city and a team together isn't.

levels.explore: Sort five examples into private and okay, with a parent.
levels.develop: Sort the whole card, and explain three choices.
levels.extend: Find a combination of okay things that together become private.

steps.title: Check settings and usernames
steps.why: Good settings and a smart username protect them even when they forget.
steps.kid: With you, your kid checks one account at a time, using the Settings check card: the username, who can see their profile, who can message them and what's public.
steps.you: Do it on your login, together. Change anything that's more open than your family rules. If they use AI with you, check its settings too: whether chats are saved, and whether they're used to train the AI.
ask: Does your username give away your real name?
Who can send you a message here?
steps.tip: A username shouldn't include your name, age, birthday or town.

levels.explore: Help a parent check one setting, and say what it does.
levels.develop: Check every account on your list, with a parent.
levels.extend: Check one account's settings for a public profile, then search for it logged out and see what a stranger sees.

steps.title: Make a privacy plan
steps.why: A plan means they know exactly what to do the next time something asks.
steps.kid: Your family writes a short privacy plan, using the What to do card, and fills in Our privacy plan at the end of the guide to keep by the computer.
steps.you: Practise a pretend moment: a game asks for their birthday. Let them say what they'd do.
ask: What will you do if a site asks for your address?
Who do you tell if a stranger messages you?
steps.tip: Stop, don't type it, ask a parent. Three steps they can remember anywhere.

levels.explore: Say the three steps: stop, don't type it, ask a parent.
levels.develop: Write the family plan together, and put it by the computer.
levels.extend: Open one app's privacy page, and find three things it collects that you never typed in, like your location or which device you use.

conclusion.headline: Their trail is mapped, and the plan is by the computer.
conclusion.text: The next time a game or site asks for something, see if they stop and come find you before typing. Stopping to ask is the whole skill.
conclusion.celebrate: When they stop and ask before sharing, say: 'You asked first. That's how your information stays yours.'
extensions: Search your family's names together, and see what comes up
Open a voice assistant's app together, if you have one, listen to what it has saved, and delete old recordings
Check whether your phone camera saves your location in photos, and turn it off together
Talk about the photos you share of them, and agree on rules together

signs: They ask before typing personal information
They pick usernames that don't give anything away
They tell you when something online asks for information
makeItReal: This week, sit down and check one of their accounts together, the username and who can see what, then put the family privacy plan by the computer.

fromHome.text: When something online asked my kids for personal information, we talked about why not to share it. Our rules: no full names, no personal information, and a username that isn't your name.

classroom.intro: Privacy works with a class when students map their own footprint privately and practise the decisions together. You run any account or settings demos on the projector, and the real settings check happens at home with family.

tips.d: Students draw their footprint map for themselves and never share real usernames, passwords or account details with the class. Group work uses made-up example accounts you provide.
Show Step 4 on the projector with a teacher account or a school platform students already use, walking through who can see what. Students never log in to personal accounts at school.
Print the Private or okay? card as cut-up slips for each group. Kids take turns placing a slip in private, okay with a parent, or fine to share, and must explain each choice.
Send home the Settings check card with a short note so families check one account together. Students without accounts can check a family member's settings with that person's permission.
Explore students draw themselves and their apps, Develop students add lines for what's linked, and Extend students circle what a stranger could find by searching, without naming anything real.
Finish with the class practising the What to do card: you read a pretend moment, like a game asking for a birthday, and students answer together: stop, don't type it, ask a grown-up.

classroom.timing: Plan two sessions of 40 to 45 minutes: Steps 1 to 3 in the first, the projector demo and Step 5 in the second. The settings check and the family privacy plan are done at home that week.
